"""
Regression test for a bug where combining a pre-init hook that accepts the
field name, a keyword-only field, and a default value on that field produced
invalid generated source code for ``__init__`` (a SyntaxError at class
creation time).

See: https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs (bug report reproduced below).
"""

import attr


def test_pre_init_with_kw_only_default_field_does_not_raise_syntax_error():
    """
    Defining a class with a pre-init hook that takes a keyword-only argument
    with a default value should not raise a SyntaxError while building the
    class, and the pre-init hook should receive the correct default value.
    """
    received = {}

    @attr.s(init=True)
    class Foo:
        kw_and_default = attr.ib(kw_only=True, default=3)

        def __attrs_pre_init__(self, *, kw_and_default):
            received["kw_and_default"] = kw_and_default

    # Class creation must succeed (no SyntaxError from the generated code).
    instance = Foo()

    # The pre-init hook must have been called with the default value.
    assert received["kw_and_default"] == 3
    assert instance.kw_and_default == 3


def test_pre_init_with_kw_only_default_field_using_define():
    """
    Same scenario but using the modern attrs.define / attr.field API, exactly
    matching the bug report's repro case.
    """
    received = {}

    @attr.define
    class Foo:
        kw_and_default: int = attr.field(kw_only=True, default=3)

        def __attrs_pre_init__(self, *, kw_and_default):
            received["kw_and_default"] = kw_and_default

    instance = Foo()

    assert received["kw_and_default"] == 3
    assert instance.kw_and_default == 3

    # Overriding the default should also work correctly and be passed
    # through to the pre-init hook.
    received.clear()
    instance2 = Foo(kw_and_default=42)

    assert received["kw_and_default"] == 42
    assert instance2.kw_and_default == 42

"""
Regression tests for the bug where a *list* of converters (which gets
turned into ``attr.setters.pipe``/``attr.Converter`` machinery) does not
behave the same way on later ``setattr`` calls as it does during
``__init__``, and where nested ``attr.Converter`` instances (using
``takes_self``/``takes_field``) inside such a list don't receive the
correct instance/field arguments.
"""

import attr


def test_list_converter_reruns_on_setattr():
    """
    A converter created from a list (e.g. ``converter=[int]``) must be
    applied again when the attribute is set after construction, just like
    it is applied during ``__init__``.
    """

    @attr.define
    class C:
        x = attr.field(converter=[int])

    c = C("1")
    assert c.x == 1

    # Re-assigning must run the same converter pipeline.
    c.x = "2"

    assert c.x == 2
    assert isinstance(c.x, int)


def test_converter_list_with_takes_self_gets_correct_arguments():
    """
    When an ``attr.Converter`` that uses ``takes_self`` is combined with
    other converters inside a list, the wrapped converter must receive the
    *actual* instance (and field) -- not some other value -- both at
    construction time and when the attribute is set again later.
    """

    def add_offset(value, instance):
        return value + instance.offset

    @attr.define
    class D:
        offset = attr.field(default=10)
        x = attr.field(
            converter=[int, attr.Converter(add_offset, takes_self=True)]
        )

    d = D(offset=10, x="5")

    assert d.x == 15  # int("5") + 10

    d.x = "7"

    assert d.x == 17  # int("7") + 10

"""
Regression test for the bug where ``__attrs_pre_init__`` receives stale /
default values instead of the actual values passed to ``__init__`` when a
class has a mixture of positional, defaulted, and keyword-only attributes.

See: https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues (pre_init argument mismatch)
"""

import attr


def test_pre_init_receives_actual_passed_values():
    captured = {}

    @attr.s(init=True)
    class MixtureClass:
        val1 = attr.ib()
        val2 = attr.ib(default=100)
        val3 = attr.ib(factory=int)
        val4 = attr.ib(kw_only=True)
        val5 = attr.ib(default=100, kw_only=True)
        val6 = attr.ib(factory=int, kw_only=True)

        def __attrs_pre_init__(self, val1, val2, val3, val4, val5, val6):
            captured["val1"] = val1
            captured["val2"] = val2
            captured["val3"] = val3
            captured["val4"] = val4
            captured["val5"] = val5
            captured["val6"] = val6

    # The pre_init hook must see exactly what was passed to the constructor,
    # matching what ends up on the instance.
    assert captured == {
        "val1": 200,
        "val2": 200,
        "val3": 200,
        "val4": 200,
        "val5": 200,
        "val6": 200,
    }

        inst.val2,
        inst.val3,

"""
Regression test for: on Python 3.14, `attr.s(auto_attribs=True)` no longer
strips out `ClassVar` attributes if the annotation ends up being a forward
reference (e.g. `typing.ForwardRef('ClassVar[str]')`) instead of the resolved
`typing.ClassVar` object.

See bug report: forward-referenced ClassVar annotations were treated as
regular attributes because `_is_class_var()` naively did `str(annot)`, which
for a `ForwardRef` object yields something like
``"ForwardRef('ClassVar[str]')"`` instead of ``"ClassVar[str]"``.
"""

import typing

import attr

from attr._make import _is_class_var


def test_is_class_var_recognizes_forward_ref():
    """
    _is_class_var() must recognize a ClassVar annotation even when it is
    represented as a typing.ForwardRef instead of a plain string or the
    resolved typing.ClassVar object.
    """
    fwd = typing.ForwardRef("ClassVar[str]")

    assert _is_class_var(fwd) is True


def test_auto_attribs_skips_forward_ref_classvar():
    """
    End-to-end: a ClassVar annotation represented as a forward reference
    must be skipped by auto_attribs, just like it is for plain strings and
    resolved typing.ClassVar objects.
    """

    class C:
        cls_var: typing.ClassVar[str]
        value: int = 1

    # Simulate the Python 3.14 behavior where the annotation ends up as a
    # forward reference object rather than the resolved ClassVar.
    C.__annotations__ = {
        "cls_var": typing.ForwardRef("ClassVar[str]"),
        "value": int,
    }

    C = attr.s(auto_attribs=True)(C)

    fields = attr.fields_dict(C)

    assert "cls_var" not in fields
    assert "value" in fields

    # Also make sure __init__ generation wasn't messed up by the bogus
    # ClassVar being treated as a real attribute.
    inst = C(value=42)
    assert inst.value == 42

"""
Regression test for a bug where frozen attrs-based exception classes
raised FrozenInstanceError when Python's exception machinery attempted
to set the ``__traceback__`` attribute (e.g. via context managers or
manual re-assignment).

See: https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues/1104
"""
from contextlib import contextmanager

import pytest

import attr
import attrs
from attr.exceptions import FrozenInstanceError


@attrs.frozen
class MyException(Exception):
    pass


@attr.s(frozen=True, auto_exc=True)
class MyOldStyleException(Exception):
    pass


@contextmanager
def do_nothing():
    yield


def test_frozen_exception_traceback_reassignment():
    """
    Manually reassigning __traceback__ on a frozen exception instance
    must not raise FrozenInstanceError.
    """
    try:
        raise MyException()
    except MyException as e:
        # This should just work -- it's normal exception machinery, not
        # user code trying to mutate a frozen field.
        e.__traceback__ = e.__traceback__


def test_frozen_exception_raised_inside_context_manager():
    """
    Raising a frozen attrs exception inside a context manager (which
    triggers traceback attachment/reattachment) must not raise
    FrozenInstanceError.
    """
    with pytest.raises(MyException):
        with do_nothing():
            raise MyException()


def test_frozen_exception_traceback_set_to_new_value():
    """
    Setting __traceback__ to a genuinely different traceback object must
    also be allowed on a frozen exception.
    """
    try:
        raise MyException()
    except MyException as e:
        tb = e.__traceback__
        # Simulate re-attaching a (possibly different) traceback, as the
        # interpreter does internally.
        e.__traceback__ = tb


def test_frozen_exception_still_frozen_for_other_attrs():
    """
    Sanity check: frozen exceptions should still forbid mutation of
    regular attributes.
    """

    @attrs.frozen
    class WithField(Exception):
        x: int

    inst = WithField(1)
    with pytest.raises(FrozenInstanceError):
        inst.x = 2


def test_old_style_frozen_exception_traceback_reassignment():
    """
    Same guarantee should hold for the classic ``attr.s`` API.
    """
    try:
        raise MyOldStyleException()
    except MyOldStyleException as e:
        e.__traceback__ = e.__traceback__

differs between Python versions because Python 3.13 automatically dedents
multi-line docstrings at compile time while earlier versions do not.

    assert doc is not None

    # ``inspect.cleandoc`` would produce -- i.e. it must not contain
    # left-over indentation from the source file's nesting level.  Before
    # the fix, running this on a Python version that does not auto-dedent
    # docstrings (< 3.13) would fail because the raw docstring text keeps

"""Regression test for IndexedSet slicing bug after pop/discard.

Bug report: IndexedSet slicing returns wrong results after any item has
been removed with pop/discard. The indices used for the slice were being
computed against the underlying storage instead of the apparent
(visible) indices, causing the slice bounds to be off after removal.
"""

from boltons.setutils import IndexedSet


def test_slice_after_pop_matches_list_semantics():
    x = IndexedSet(range(10))
    x.pop(2)  # remove element with value 2

    expected_list = list(range(10))
    expected_list.pop(2)

    assert list(x) == expected_list

    # This is the exact case from the bug report
    assert list(x[1:4]) == expected_list[1:4]


def test_slice_after_discard_matches_list_semantics():
    x = IndexedSet(range(10))
    x.discard(2)

    expected_list = list(range(10))
    expected_list.remove(2)

    assert list(x) == expected_list
    assert list(x[1:4]) == expected_list[1:4]
    assert list(x[:5]) == expected_list[:5]
    assert list(x[2:]) == expected_list[2:]


def test_slice_with_negative_indices_after_removal():
    x = IndexedSet(range(10))
    x.pop(2)

    expected_list = list(range(10))
    expected_list.pop(2)

    assert list(x[-5:-1]) == expected_list[-5:-1]
    assert list(x[1:-1]) == expected_list[1:-1]
    assert list(x[-8:8]) == expected_list[-8:8]

import pytest

from boltons.setutils import IndexedSet


def test_getitem_negative_out_of_range_raises_index_error():
    x = IndexedSet(range(10))
    x.pop(2)  # len is now 9, causing dead index bookkeeping

    assert len(x) == 9
    # valid negative index still works
    assert x[-1] == 9

    # way out of range negative index must raise IndexError, not wrap around
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        x[-10]

    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        x[-15]

    x = IndexedSet(range(10))
    x.pop(2)  # len is now 9

    assert len(x) == 9

    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        x.pop(-15)

    # the pop attempt should not have silently removed some unrelated element
    assert 4 in x
    assert len(x) == 9

    # smallest valid negative index (-9) should be the first element
    val = x[-9]
    assert val == list(x)[0]

"""
Regression tests for boltons.jsonutils.JSONLIterator hanging forever
when:
  1) rel_seek lands inside the last line of a file lacking a trailing
     newline, and
  2) a negative rel_seek value is supplied (which should seek relative
     to the end of the file, like negative indices do).

Both scenarios used to spin forever in `_align_to_newline` (an infinite
loop reading empty strings at EOF). These tests use a background
thread with a timeout so that a hang causes a clean test failure
instead of blocking the whole test run indefinitely.
"""

import json
import queue
import threading

import pytest

from boltons.jsonutils import JSONLIterator


def _run_with_timeout(func, timeout=5):
    """Runs func() in a daemon thread. Returns (finished, result_or_exc).

    If the thread doesn't finish within `timeout` seconds, returns
    (False, None) without blocking the calling thread further (the
    worker thread is left running as a daemon).
    """
    q = queue.Queue()

    def target():
        try:
            result = func()
        except BaseException as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - capture anything
            result = e
        q.put(result)

    t = threading.Thread(target=target, daemon=True)
    t.start()
    t.join(timeout)
    if t.is_alive():
        return False, None
    return True, q.get_nowait()


def test_rel_seek_no_trailing_newline_does_not_hang(tmp_path):
    """rel_seek landing inside the final (newline-less) line must not
    cause the iterator to hang forever -- it should either complete
    normally or raise a clear exception, but never spin indefinitely.
    """
    path = tmp_path / "no_trailing_newline.jsonl"
    path.write_text('{"1": 1}\n{"2": 2}')

    def do_iter():
        with open(path) as f:
            it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=0.9)
            return list(it)

    finished, _result = _run_with_timeout(do_iter, timeout=5)

    assert finished, (
        "JSONLIterator hung when rel_seek landed inside the last line "
        "of a file without a trailing newline"
    )


def test_negative_rel_seek_seeks_from_end_and_does_not_hang(tmp_path):
    """A negative rel_seek should behave like negative indexing: it
    should seek relative to the end of the file (equivalent to
    `1.0 + rel_seek` as a positive fraction), not overflow past the
    end of the file and hang.
    """
    path = tmp_path / "normal.jsonl"
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        for i in range(20):
            f.write(json.dumps({"n": i}) + "\n")

    def do_iter_pos():
        with open(path) as f:
            it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=0.5)
            return list(it)

    def do_iter_neg():
        with open(path) as f:
            it = JSONLIterator(f, rel_seek=-0.5)
            return list(it)

    finished_pos, pos_result = _run_with_timeout(do_iter_pos, timeout=5)
    assert finished_pos, "baseline positive rel_seek unexpectedly hung"
    assert isinstance(pos_result, list), (
        "positive rel_seek=0.5 raised an unexpected exception: %r" % (pos_result,)
    )

    finished_neg, neg_result = _run_with_timeout(do_iter_neg, timeout=5)

    assert finished_neg, (
        "JSONLIterator hung with a negative rel_seek value instead of "
        "seeking relative to the end of the file"
    )
    assert isinstance(neg_result, list), (
        "negative rel_seek=-0.5 raised an unexpected exception: %r" % (neg_result,)
    )

    # -0.5 should be equivalent to seeking from the end the same
    # relative distance as +0.5 from the start of the file.
    assert neg_result == pos_result

"""Regression test for cachetools issue where create_autospec on a class
using @cachedmethod raises AttributeError because mock introspects class
attributes with obj=None, which triggers the descriptor's __get__ logic.
"""

import unittest.mock

import pytest

from cachetools import LRUCache, cachedmethod


class Cached:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cache = LRUCache(maxsize=10)

    @cachedmethod(lambda self: self.cache)
    def get(self, key):
        return key


def test_create_autospec_instance_does_not_raise():
    # This used to raise AttributeError from deep inside the descriptor
    # logic because unittest.mock passes None as the instance when
    # introspecting class-level attributes.
    mock_obj = unittest.mock.create_autospec(Cached, instance=True)
    assert mock_obj is not None


def test_create_autospec_class_does_not_raise():
    mock_cls = unittest.mock.create_autospec(Cached)
    assert mock_cls is not None


def test_getattr_on_class_does_not_raise():
    # More directly: accessing the descriptor via the class (obj=None)
    # should not raise AttributeError, mirroring what mock's introspection
    # does internally (e.g. checking for iscoroutinefunction etc.).
    try:
        attr = Cached.get
    except AttributeError as exc:
        pytest.fail(f"Accessing cachedmethod via class raised AttributeError: {exc}")
    assert attr is not None

"""
Regression test for the requested ``more_itertools.synchronized`` helper.

The feature request asks for a decorator (analogous to ``serialize``) that
can wrap a generator function so that calling ``next()`` on the resulting
generator from multiple threads simultaneously is safe -- i.e. it behaves
like a single serialized stream of values with no corruption, no lost
values, no duplicated values, and no exceptions raised due to concurrent
execution of the same generator.
"""

import threading
import time

import pytest

import more_itertools as mi


def test_synchronized_exists():
    """The library should expose a ``synchronized`` decorator."""
    assert hasattr(mi, 'synchronized'), (
        "more_itertools has no attribute 'synchronized'"
    )


def test_synchronized_decorator_usage():
    """``synchronized`` should be usable as a plain decorator on a
    generator function, similar to ``consumer``."""

    @mi.synchronized
    def counter():
        i = 0
        while True:
            yield i
            i += 1

    it = counter()
    # The wrapped generator should still behave like a normal iterator.
    assert next(it) == 0
    assert next(it) == 1
    assert next(it) == 2


def test_synchronized_is_thread_safe():
    """Calling next() concurrently from multiple threads on a generator
    wrapped with ``synchronized`` must not raise errors, and must yield
    every produced value exactly once."""

    N = 60

    def gen():
        for i in range(N):
            # Give other threads a chance to race for this generator's
            # execution slot while it's doing "work" between yields.
            time.sleep(0.001)
            yield i

    synced = mi.synchronized(gen)()

    results = []
    results_lock = threading.Lock()
    errors = []

    def worker():
        while True:
            try:
                value = next(synced)
            except StopIteration:
                return
            except BaseException as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                errors.append(exc)
                return
            with results_lock:
                results.append(value)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(8)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join(timeout=10)

    assert not errors, f"Concurrent access raised errors: {errors!r}"
    # Every value from 0..N-1 must have been produced exactly once, with
    # nothing lost or duplicated due to unsynchronized concurrent access.
    assert sorted(results) == list(range(N))

"""
Regression test for running_min / running_max not preserving which
element was actually picked when values compare equal but have
different types.

Python's builtin min()/max() are stable: when two values compare equal,
the *first* one encountered is returned. running_min() and running_max()
with a sliding window (maxlen given) should behave the same way, since
they are meant to be windowed generalizations of min()/max().
"""

from fractions import Fraction

import more_itertools as mi


def test_running_min_preserves_first_equal_element_type():
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]

    result_types = [type(x) for x in mi.running_min(data, maxlen=2)]

    # What plain, stable min() would produce for the same windows:
    #   window 0: [0]                -> min -> int
    #   window 1: [0, 0.0]           -> min -> int (first arg wins on tie)
    #   window 2: [0.0, Fraction(0)] -> min -> float (first arg wins on tie)
    expected_types = [
        type(min(data[0:1])),
        type(min(data[0:2])),
        type(min(data[1:3])),
    ]

    assert result_types == expected_types


def test_running_max_preserves_first_equal_element_type():
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]

    result_types = [type(x) for x in mi.running_max(data, maxlen=2)]

    expected_types = [
        type(max(data[0:1])),
        type(max(data[0:2])),
        type(max(data[1:3])),
    ]

    assert result_types == expected_types


def test_running_min_values_still_correct():
    # Sanity check: even though the *identity*/type of the chosen equal
    # element changed, the numeric value returned must still be correct.
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]
    result = list(mi.running_min(data, maxlen=2))
    assert result == [0, 0, 0]


def test_running_max_values_still_correct():
    data = [0, 0.0, Fraction(0)]
    result = list(mi.running_max(data, maxlen=2))
    assert result == [0, 0, 0]

from semver import Version

"""
Regression test for the bug where `tabulate(..., maxcolwidths=...)` raises an
exception when a cell contains a "True"/"False" string or a None value.

See bug report: using maxcolwidths on a table containing a boolean-like string
cell ("True"/"False") or a None cell crashes instead of producing wrapped
output.
"""

import pytest

from tabulate import tabulate


def test_maxcolwidths_with_boolean_string_and_none_does_not_raise():
    """The exact repro from the bug report should not raise, and should
    render "True" as plain text and None as a blank cell."""
    data = [
        ["First Entry", "True"],
        ["Second Entry", None],
    ]
    headers = ["Title", "When"]

    # This used to raise an exception (TypeError/AttributeError) inside
    # _wrap_text_to_colwidths.
    result = tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt="grid", maxcolwidths=[7, 5])

    # "True" should show up as literal text somewhere in the output.
    assert "True" in result

    # None should be rendered as a blank cell, not crash and not print "None".
    assert "None" not in result


def test_maxcolwidths_wide_enough_matches_unwrapped_output():
    """When maxcolwidths is large enough that no actual wrapping occurs,
    the output should be identical to calling tabulate without
    maxcolwidths at all. This pins down that "True"/"False" strings and
    None values are cast/handled the same way with or without the
    maxcolwidths code path."""
    data = [
        ["First Entry", "True"],
        ["Second Entry", None],
        ["Third Entry", "False"],
    ]
    headers = ["Title", "When"]

    expected = tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt="grid")

    # width 20 is larger than any cell content, so no wrapping should
    # actually happen -- output should match the unwrapped table exactly.
    actual = tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt="grid", maxcolwidths=[20, 20])

    assert actual == expected
